newsitem.title: FRANCE: Gambler Chirac could regret playing election card.
newsitem.headline: Gambler Chirac could regret playing election card.

text.p: With the first round of France's parliamentary election three days away, President Jacques Chirac may be wondering if he is going to regret one of the biggest gambles of his political career -- calling a snap poll.

The impulsive 64-year-old leader, nicknamed "the bulldozer," called the election 10 months early ostensibly to gain a free hand for his drive to build a strong, united Europe with a single currency and a major leadership role for himself.
Some said Chirac brought the election forward because France would need to make further painful public spending cuts later this year to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The cuts would affect the country's generous social welfare system and irate voters would vent their anger by voting against pro-government candidates in the March poll, the argument ran.

But the brief campaign has suggested Chirac may have misjudged voter feelings and his supporters may be made to pay now for an uncertain economic situation as well as for what many French people feel was a cynical political ploy.

Opinion polls show many voters already intend to use their ballots to punish the government for what they see as a poor performance since Chirac glided into office in May 1995 on a cascade of mostly-unfulfilled promises.

No poll published before last Saturday's midnight blackout forecast the left would win the May 25-June 1 election, but many suggested the centre-right could lose up to 150 or even more of its 464 seats in the 577-member National Assembly.
Aides say Chirac knew the campaign would be difficult and called the election now to reduce the potential losses.
But he may have miscalculated, as he appeared to do when he handpicked his long-time aide Edouard Balladur to be prime minister after the centre-right won a general election in 1993.

Ailing Socialist president Francois Mitterrand was still in office and Chirac, who had served as premier under Mitterrand in 1986-88, feared he would lose his own popularity ahead of the 1995 presidential vote if he "cohabited" with Mitterrand again.
However the caretaker Balladur, buoyed by early successes, decided to run for the presidency himself and was only narrowly outmanoeuvered when he tried to force Chirac out of the race.

Chirac has used his position, with a trade-boosting trip to China and high-profile European diplomacy, to influence the current campaign, warning that France could be weakened if the left-wing opposition wins and "cohabits" with him.

Chirac's hand, or that of his image makers, has loomed heavily over the way the centre-right coalition has run its campaign, not leastly in the use of the insistent word "elan", which means impulse, forward movement or momentum.
The ruling coalition's slogan, "With Jacques Chirac, a shared elan" has delighted satirists, not leastly because elan also means "elk", the cousin of a moose.

The satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine depicted the two parties in the ruling centre-right coalition as a pair of elks mating while others recalled that reference to the antlers of such animals are a coded reference in French for being a cuckold.

A defeat for his supporters could make Chirac not an elk but a lame duck president for much of the rest of a seven-year term which ends in 2002, dashing his ambition to be the strong leader of Europe at the turn of the millenium.
But Chirac, who prides himself on being a pragmatist, has a dogged determination and friend and foe alike say that in the end, he always manages to bounce back.
